deep.reconstruction:
The page is one sheet of a large hand-ruled table that runs across several folios. The previous folio has column primes 97 to 223. This folio has 227 to 359. The next folio has 367 to 503.

Layout:
- The 24 column headers, repeated at the foot, are the consecutive primes q = 227, 229, 233, 239, 241, 251, 257, 263, 269, 271, 277, 281, 283, 293, 307, 311, 313, 317, 331, 337, 347, 349, 353, 359. Heavy rules group them in sixes.
- The sheet is cut into horizontal blocks. Only the lowest block is used. Its row labels are primes p between 950 and 1000: 953, a faint 971, 977, 983, 991, 997. The prime 967 is absent.
- Rows 953 and 971 are empty. Small circles are entered only in rows 977, 983, 991 and 997.

What the circles mean. I tested this by computing Legendre symbols with quadratic reciprocity, cell by cell. A circle in row p, column q means (q/p) = +1, that is, the column prime q is a quadratic residue modulo the row prime p.
- For p = 977 (≡ 1 mod 4) the direction does not matter.
- For p = 983 and 991 (≡ 3 mod 4) it does, and it settles the question. For example, (983/251) = −1 but (251/983) = +1, and 251 is circled in row 983. Likewise (991/239) = −1 but (239/991) = +1, and 239 is circled in row 991.

So the page is a strip of a table of quadratic characters: moduli p are the primes 953–997, and the residues tested are the primes q. It is a large extension, in form, of the tables of quadratic residues at the end of Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (Tabula II).

Circled cells read from the image, each confirmed by computation:
- Row 977: 227, 229, 269, 271, 277, 313, 317, 349, 353.
- Row 983: 233, 251, 263, 269, 281, 293, 313, 337, 349, 353, 359.
- Row 991: 227, 229, 239, 241, 251, 263, 277, 283, 311, 313, 349, 353.
- Row 997: 227, 229, 257, 263, 269, 307, 311, 313, 331, 337.

The connecting lines. Short horizontal and vertical strokes join circles that sit in adjacent columns or adjacent rows. Examples:
- the 2×2 square at 227/229 × 991/997;
- the chain 269–271–277 in row 977, dropping through 269 (row 983) to 263 in rows 983, 991 and 997, and on to 257 and 269 in row 997;
- the square block at 349/353 over rows 977–991, with a spur to 359 in row 983.

These strokes are a purely graphical aid. They make the residue pattern visible and easy to check; they carry no arithmetic content.

Method I assume (mine): each entry was obtained by reducing p mod q and evaluating (p mod q / q). Reciprocity, with its sign for p, q ≡ 3 mod 4, then converts this to (q/p). Equivalently, one could list the quadratic residues mod p directly.
errors: Probable omission: (317/991) = +1. Indeed 991 ≡ 40 (mod 317), (2/317) = −1 and (5/317) = −1, so (40/317) = +1, and 317 ≡ 1 (mod 4). The cell row 991 / column 317 should therefore carry a circle. In the image the 307–317 cluster shows 317 circled only in row 977, so Gauss appears to have missed this entry (or the mark is too faint to see).
Every other cell in rows 977, 983, 991 and 997 agrees with the computed Legendre symbols, both marked and unmarked.
Rows 953 and 971 are left blank, and the row for 967 is missing altogether. The table is incomplete rather than wrong.

results.what: Table of quadratic characters (q/p) for row moduli p ∈ {977, 983, 991, 997} (953 and 971 ruled but empty) and prime arguments q from 227 to 359. A circle marks a quadratic residue. The sheet is part of a multi-folio table covering q from about 97 to 503.
results.modern_name: Table of Legendre symbols / quadratic residue table
results.usually_credited_to: Legendre (1798) and Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae 1801, Tabula II) for the first such tables; extensive tables later by Jacobi (Canon Arithmeticus, 1839) and others

results.what: Graphical linking of adjacent residue entries into connected clusters, as a visual or checking aid
results.modern_name: none (visual aid; resembles plotting a residue pattern)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss is well known to have computed extensive quadratic residue tables, both in the Disquisitiones and in his Nachlass. This page is a routine, largely correct strip of such a table for moduli near 1000. The only mildly notable features are its range and the line-drawing visualization.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import primerange; from sympy.ntheory import legendre_symbol; [q for q in primerange(227,360) if legendre_symbol(q,977)==1] == [227,229,269,271,277,313,317,349,353]
checkable.asserts: Row 977 circles are exactly the primes 227..359 that are quadratic residues mod 977

transcription_corrections: The left margin carries a faint row label 971 between 953 and 977. The machine transcription omits it, and the row is empty. The prime 967 has no row.
The circles mean 'column prime is a quadratic residue of the row prime'. The lines join horizontally or vertically adjacent circles.
